# Conditional Schwarz reduction for a rank-deficient cap cover

This is an exact symmetry reduction in the positive mixed-volume case.
It preserves a selected whole-space cap cover and its original constant
`gamma_d`. It also permits a consistent normal stress to be reselected
after symmetry. It does not lower the continuous dimension appearing
in that constant.

## 1. The real-slice construction and convexity

Let `C subset R^n x R^d` be a convex body. Suppose the continuous
normals of a selected finite ambient cap family belong to a subspace
`V subset R^d`, of dimension `1<=r<d`. Set `W=V^perp` and `m=d-r`.
Write the continuous coordinate as `x=v+w`, with `v in V,w in W`.
Only this orthogonal continuous coordinate change is used; it leaves
`Z^n x R^d` unchanged and has absolute determinant one.

Let `B` be the real projection of `C` onto `R^n x V`. For `p=(z,v)`
in `B`, define its nonempty compact convex slice

`D_p={w in W:(z,v+w) in C}`,
`f(p)=vol_m(D_p)`, `R(p)=(f(p)/kappa_m)^(1/m)`.

Here `kappa_m` is the volume of the unit ball in `W`. Slices with
zero m-volume have radius zero, rather than being removed from the
projection. Brunn-Minkowski and the slice inclusion from convexity give

`R((1-t)p+tq)>=(1-t)R(p)+t R(q)` for `p,q in B`, `0<=t<=1`. (1)

The radius is upper semicontinuous on the compact convex projection.
Indeed, along convergent base points, every Hausdorff limit of their
bounded slices is contained in the limiting slice. Volume continuity
for compact convex sets, including zero-volume limits, then gives the
required upper bound on the limsup. Define

`C^*={(z,v+w):(z,v) in B, |w|<=R(z,v)}`.                    (2)

Upper semicontinuity makes this set closed; it is bounded, and (1)
plus the triangle inequality makes it convex. It has nonempty ambient
interior because an interior ball of `C` supplies positive-radius
slices over an open set in `R^n x V`. Thus `C^*` is again a convex
body. Its entire real projection `B`, including zero-radius boundary
slices, is unchanged.

## 2. Exact mixed measure and selected-cap identities

Assume `M=H_d(C intersect (Z^n x R^d))>0`. Thus the intrinsic
dimension of the original mixed set is `q=d`. For every integer z,
ordinary orthogonal Fubini gives

`vol_d(C_z)=integral_V f(z,v) dv=vol_d(C_z^*)`.               (3)

Nonempty and positive-volume integer-fiber index sets are separately
preserved. Nonemptiness follows from equality of the real projection;
positive volume follows from (3). In particular `q=d` and total mass
`M` remain unchanged.

Every selected margin has the form

`L_i(z,v+w)=a_i dot z+u_i dot v-b_i`, `u_i in V`.

For every Borel function `Phi(z,v)` for which either side is defined,

`integral_(C intersect Lambda) Phi(z,v) dH_d
 =sum_(z in Z^n) integral_V Phi(z,v) f(z,v) dv
 =integral_(C^* intersect Lambda) Phi(z,v) dH_d`.             (4)

All sums are finite. In particular (4) preserves total mass, every
selected CLOSED cap mass, every selected hinge, every integer first
moment, and every projected continuous cap first moment. It also
preserves these quantities for EVERY perturbation of cap parameters
whose continuous normals remain in `V`, not only at the selected
family. Every selected cap boundary has zero d-volume on each fiber,
since its continuous normal is nonzero, but the identity for the
closed cap itself does not require removing any base-boundary fiber.

Whole-space coverage above any specified integer indices is unchanged:
the affine margins did not change at any point of the ambient space.
Thus an original cover whose cap ratios are below a prescribed number
has exactly the same ratios on `C^*`, with exactly the same cap count.

The reduced source is the measure

`d mu_red(z,v)=f(z,v) dv` on `Z^n x V`,

supported in the convex real set `B`, with
`f^(1/m)=kappa_m^(1/m) R` concave there. This is an exact
`1/m`-concave density. Its target remains

`gamma_(r+m)/2^n=gamma_d/2^n`,                              (5)

and is not replaced by `gamma_r/2^n`. In particular this is not yet
an induction which removes `m` continuous dimensions.

## 3. Proper sections and the nonsmooth stress issue

If a selected cap plane cuts a source fiber properly, orthogonal
coarea gives

`H_(d-1)(C_z intersect {L_i=0})
 =integral_(v in V, L_i(z,v)=0) f(z,v) dH_(r-1)(v)`.        (6)

The same identity holds for `C^*`. It preserves the proper section
mass and the integer and V-projected section first moments. In the
symmetric body every perpendicular section first moment is zero.
The factor `1/|u_i|` in a cap-volume derivative is unchanged; with
unit continuous normalization it is one.

At supporting-facet coincidences an effective section gradient can
have a measurable density in `[0,1]`. Pushing forward an arbitrary
old density and distributing it radially would preserve its listed
moments, but does NOT by itself prove that it is a realizable new-body
generalized gradient. The following reselection avoids that inference.

Suppose the selected cover is an attained regular-budget minimizer
in the unframed whole-space setting, with normal span `V`, as in
the rank-stratum normality theorem (candidate da91e18223378a53).
Rerun its exact-penalty proof using only continuous normals in fixed
`V`, without the common rotation variables. By (4), every source cap
mass and hinge function in this parameter family is IDENTICAL for
`C` and `C^*`; coverage is also identical. The selected cover is
therefore still a minimizing cover within this restricted parameter
family on the symmetric source. The original global value function
still supplies the same local lower bound and exact sensitivity in
the penalty argument. It is not asserted to be the unrestricted
global value for the new symmetric source.

This yields objective-one multipliers, actual whole-space contact
measures in `V`, and consistent restricted cap gradients with

`M sum_i r_i=-v_original'(tau)`.                            (7)

These restricted gradients can be lifted to consistent physical
cap gradients for the symmetric source, with perpendicular moment
zero. Here is the nonsmooth justification. The inclusion of the
fixed-V cap parameters into the full physical parameters is smooth;
the locally Lipschitz generalized-gradient composition inclusion puts
every selected restricted gradient in the projection of the compact
convex physical gradient set. Choose one lift. Reflection in `W`
preserves the symmetric source and all cap parameters with normal in
`V`. It preserves that physical gradient set, fixes its offset,
integer, and V-normal components, and negates its perpendicular
normal component. Average the lift with its reflection. The result
is an actual member of the same convex generalized-gradient set,
retains every selected restricted component, and has perpendicular
normal component zero. Sphere charts cause no gap: one may first
work with arbitrary nonzero normals in `V` and retain the smooth
unit-norm equation; the restriction map is then a linear inclusion
in all the normal, base, and offset coordinates.

Every such physical gradient has the consistent coarea density
representation already proved in the normality note. Thus this
argument supplies realizable new-body section data, rather than
arbitrary independently assigned facet moments. Its perpendicular
section first moment is zero. The ordinary cap perpendicular first
moment is also zero by conditional reflection symmetry.

## 4. The normal source tensor after symmetry

Use the reselected data from Section 3 and let

`W_i=c_i+r_i S_i`,
`T=sum_i (X_i+r_i X_i^s)u_i^T`,
`Q=sum_i Psi_i u_i u_i^T`.

The restricted normal stress gives the same mass/base equations and
the V-projected continuous equations as before. Their contacts can
be chosen in `V`. Since the new source cap and section perpendicular
moments vanish, these projected equations now have zero perpendicular
components on both sides. In particular the symmetric source has

`sum_i W_i u_i=0`,
`sum_i u_i(Z_i+r_i Z_i^s)^T=0`,
`T=Q`.                                                     (8)

The right-hand tensor `Q`, and every individual `Psi_i`, are numerically
unchanged from the selected cap family. The individual multipliers
and supporting-facet trace densities may have been reselected; it is
their total sensitivity (7), not an arbitrary original trace choice,
which is retained. All the displayed section data are realizable
gradients for the new source. No claim of unrestricted new-body
minimality, or of contact membership in its source fibers, is made.

## 5. Why the intrinsic lower-dimensional case needs its own reduction

The m-volume slice construction cannot simply replace `H_d` by the
intrinsic `H_q` when `q<d`. Here is an explicit failure. Let `n=1,d=2`,
with continuous coordinates `(v,w)`, and let

`C=conv( {0} x {(s,s):-1<=s<=1}
          union {1} x {(t,0):-1<=t<=1} )`.

It is a full three-dimensional convex body: the two segments at
different base indices have independent continuous directions. Its
only integer fibers are those two segments, so `q=1`. Their intrinsic
lengths are `2sqrt(2)` and `2`.

Take `V` to be the v-axis and symmetrize one-dimensional w-slices.
At each endpoint integer index every such slice is a singleton, of
one-dimensional volume zero. The symmetric integer fibers are both
the horizontal segment `[-1,1] x {0}`, each of intrinsic length two.
Thus even the normalized weights of the two integer fibers change.

Consequently (3)--(8) are statements in the positive `H_d` case.
An intrinsic lower-dimensional instance must first use a separately
proved degeneracy reduction; this note does not supply or presume
an intrinsic measure identity for the Schwarz operation itself.
